Let’s talk about something that really hits home for anyone who’s ever tried to live close to the land.
Chapter Fourteen—Rethinking Success: What Does “Living with Nature” Really Mean?
Picture a young couple, brand new to rural life. They’re doing their best, but suddenly, mice are darting around in the pantry, and deer are munching away in the garden. At first, they’re determined to fix every problem—setting traps, spraying repellents, building fences. They want everything just right.
But pretty soon, reality sets in. The mice keep coming back. The deer always find a new way to sneak in. No matter what they do, something else pops up. And what happens? They start to realize that chasing perfection is a losing battle.
So, they shift their thinking. Instead of trying to control every little thing, they focus on what really matters. They protect their favorite vegetables, accept a few nibbled leaves, and start enjoying the garden as a place that’s full of life—unexpected, sometimes messy, but always interesting.
Or think about a park manager, responsible for a huge nature reserve. She’s got people telling her to fix this, stop that, solve every problem. But deep down, she knows the truth: some conflicts just can’t be eliminated. Her job isn’t to make everything perfect. It’s to keep things in balance, so both people and wildlife can thrive—even if that means living with a bit of tension.
Here’s something to pay attention to—most of us don’t realize how much our own expectations shape what we feel. If we expect a tidy, orderly world, every mess feels like failure. But if we accept that some things will always be a little wild, we find so much more peace.
So, what’s the real lesson here? Living with nature isn’t about winning or losing. It’s about sharing space, making compromises, and finding joy in all the unpredictability that comes with a world that’s truly alive.
The garden might never be perfect, but it will be a place full of stories—and that’s a different kind of success.
